'''Charles Santori''' is an American [[physicist]]. He obtained his Bachelor of Science degree from MIT in 1997 and then got his Ph.D. in [[applied physics]] from [[Stanford University]] six years later after finishing his studies on [[semiconductor]]s with Professor [[Yoshihisa Yamamoto (scientist)|Yoshihisa Yamamoto]]. In 2005 Charles joined [[HP Labs]] where he researches diamond photonics.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hpl.hp.com/people/charles_santori/|title=Charles Santori|publisher=[[HP Labs]]|accessdate=April 22, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100608104318/http://www.hpl.hp.com/people/charles_santori/|archive-date=June 8, 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> A year before his graduation from Stanford he along with other classmates of Yamamoto team invented [[quantum cryptography]] that used [[photon]] turnstile device.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Secure communication: Quantum cryptography with a photon turnstile|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=420|issue=6917|page=762|year=2002|doi=10.1038/420762a|bibcode = 2002Natur.420..762W|pmid=12490939 | last1 = Waks | first1 = E | last2 = Inoue | first2 = K | last3 = Santori | first3 = C | last4 = Fattal | first4 = D | last5 = Vuckovic | first5 = J | last6 = Solomon | first6 = GS | last7 = Yamamoto | first7 = Y| doi-access = free }}</ref> The same year, he published one of his most cited works on indistinguishable photons called ''Indistinguishable photons from a single-photon device''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rcmOxu8AAAAJ&hl=en|title=Charles Santori|publisher=[[Google Scholar]]|accessdate=April 22, 2015}}</ref>
